nodes.content: Characterize when heterogeneous treatment effects remain partially identifiable with weak instruments and bounded exclusion violations in observational healthcare.
requirements: Achieve at least 95% confidence-set coverage uniformly over specified instrument-strength and exclusion-violation classes.
Establish sharp identification bounds and characterize when they improve upon bounds without instruments.

nodes.content: Derive sharp stratified-effect LP bounds under bounded exclusion violations; compare no-IV widths and invert uniformly valid 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests.
At what exclusion-risk slack does a ≤5-point physician-preference first stage stop narrowing comorbidity-specific 30-day readmission bounds versus no-IV?
With a five-point physician-preference first stage, exclusion slack under one risk point narrows comorbidity-specific bounds; five points eliminates no-IV gains.
Grid 0–5-point first stages and exclusion slack; compare stratified LP bounds against no-IV and invert 95% weak-IV-robust moment tests.
Simulate 10,000 cohorts of 2,000 patients per 0–5-point first-stage/slack cell; compare LP versus no-IV widths and 95% weak-IV coverage.
At five-point first stage and 0.5-point slack, high-comorbidity LP width matched no-IV (100 points); minimum coverage was 95.1%.
Re-solve high-comorbidity LPs at 0–1-point slack, compare no-IV widths, and verify extremal witnesses at five-point first stage.
At 0.1-point slack, high-comorbidity LP width was 96 versus 100 points without instruments; constructed distributions attained both endpoints.
Can negative-control-calibrated exclusion slack preserve uniform 95% coverage as the physician-preference first stage approaches zero?
Use 0.5-point no-gain and 0.1-point sharpness results to calibrate negative-control slack; invert uncertainty-adjusted 95% tests near zero first stage.
Calibrate slack via negative-control upper bounds, using 0.1-point sharpness and 0.5-point no-gain anchors; simulate worst-cell 95% coverage near zero.
WeakIV-NC v1 notebook contains negative-control slack calibration and worst-cell confidence-set coverage tables for 0–0.5-point first stages.
Enumerate response types under monotone prescribing and bounded direct effects; derive sharp subgroup bounds and weak-IV-robust confidence sets.
At a five-point first stage, does monotone prescribing narrow high-comorbidity bounds at 0.5-point slack despite unrestricted LP no-gain?
At five-point first stage and 0.5-point slack, monotone prescribing lowers high-comorbidity width to ≤95 versus 100 points unrestricted.
Enumerate monotone-prescribing response types and solve high-comorbidity LPs at five-point first stage, 0.5-point slack; verify endpoint witnesses.
Monotone-prescribing LP yielded 93-point high-comorbidity width versus 100 unrestricted; feasible response-type mixtures attained both endpoints.
Derive joint two-instrument bounded-exclusion LP bounds using physician preference and formulary access; invert weak-IV-robust tests for 95% coverage.
Calibrate both exclusion slacks from negative controls; invert joint weak-IV tests at zero physician first stage, checking worst-case 95% coverage.
Extend WeakIV-NC v1 with joint physician/formulary weak-IV simulations, negative-control slack calibration, and worst-case 95% coverage at zero physician first stage.
WeakIV-NC v2 notebook adds joint physician/formulary LP endpoint witnesses and worst-cell coverage tables at zero physician first stage.
Audit WeakIV-NC v2 endpoint witnesses; simulate 10,000 zero-physician-first-stage cohorts, comparing joint-LP versus no-IV widths and 95% coverage.
At zero physician first stage, high-comorbidity joint LP width was 94 versus 100 no-IV points; minimum coverage 95.2%, endpoints attained.
Simulate correlated physician/formulary instruments across 0–5-point first stages and 0–1-point exclusion slacks; audit joint-LP sharpness and worst-cell 95% coverage.
With instrument correlation 0.8, 0.5-point first stages and slacks yielded 92.9% worst-cell coverage, below 95%.
Can covariance-aware critical values restore 95% coverage at instrument correlation 0.8 while retaining narrower-than-no-IV high-comorbidity bounds?
Calibrate covariance-aware critical values across first-stage/slack grids at ρ=0.8; resimulate coverage and compare high-comorbidity confidence-set widths against no-IV.
Using the 94-point width and 92.9% coverage results, recalibrate critical values at ρ=0.8; simulate worst-cell coverage and no-IV widths.
WeakIV-NC v3 records covariance-aware critical values, ρ=0.8 worst-cell coverage, and high-comorbidity width comparisons against no-IV.
Project simultaneous 95% frequency-and-slack regions through sharp response-type LPs; benchmark no-IV widths without first-stage division or independence assumptions.
Construct covariance-aware simultaneous frequency/slack regions at ρ=0.8; project through response-type LPs, then test worst-cell coverage and no-IV width.
Reanalyze WeakIV-NC v3’s ρ=0.8 cohorts with simultaneous-region projection; compare worst-cell coverage, sharp endpoint witnesses, and no-IV widths.
At ρ=0.8, projected sets achieved 95.3% worst-cell coverage and 98-point median width versus 100 no-IV points; LP endpoints attained.
Stress-test projected sets across 0–5-point first stages, 0–1-point slacks, and correlations 0–0.8; audit 95% coverage and sharpness.
At zero first stages, one-point slacks, and ρ=0.6, projected sets covered only 93.8% in sparse high-comorbidity strata.
Project exact multinomial confidence regions and Bonferroni-calibrated exclusion slacks through response-type LPs; benchmark sharp bounds against no-IV.
Do exact multinomial regions restore ≥95% sparse-stratum coverage without erasing the two-point width gain observed at ρ=0.8?
Exact multinomial projection raises sparse-stratum minimum coverage above 95% while retaining median width below 100 no-IV points at ρ=0.8.
Invert exact multinomial tests in sparse strata, Bonferroni-adjust slack calibration, and compare projected-set coverage and width against no-IV.
Run 10,000 sparse-stratum exact-multinomial projections at zero first stages, one-point slacks, and ρ=0.6/0.8; compare coverage and no-IV widths.
Exact projection restored minimum sparse-stratum coverage to 95.1% across ρ=0.6/0.8; at ρ=0.8 median width was 99 versus 100 no-IV points.
Using 95.1% sparse-stratum coverage, audit exact projections across 0–5-point stages, 0–1-point slacks, and ρ≤0.8; verify sharpness and no-IV gains.
Gridwide minimum coverage was 95.1%; feasible witnesses attained LP endpoints; five-point stage/0.1-point slack yielded 96-point bounds versus 100 no-IV.
Enumerate LP dual certificates across physician/formulary first-stage and slack pairs to locate sharp no-IV improvement thresholds by comorbidity stratum.
At 2.7-point physician stage/0.23-point slack, an omitted joint-instrument facet reduced p5’s 98-point LP width to 95, refuting sharpness.
Which joint-instrument facets tighten p5’s bounds beyond the 2.7-point stage/0.23-point slack example, and preserve exact-projection coverage?
Enumerate omitted joint-instrument facets, add them to exact-projection LPs, verify endpoint witnesses, and rerun gridwide 95% coverage checks.
Add the 2.7-stage/0.23-slack facet to exact-projection LPs; enumerate other joint facets, certify endpoints, and recheck gridwide 95% coverage.
JointFacet-LP v1 contains enumerated joint-instrument facets, endpoint-witness certificates, and exact-projection coverage tables across the first-stage/slack grid.
Independently audit JointFacet-LP v1 facets and endpoint witnesses; rerun 10,000-cohort simulations for 95% coverage and no-IV-width comparisons.
Audit confirmed endpoint witnesses and 95-point width versus prior 98 and no-IV 100; minimum simulated gridwide coverage was 95.1%.
Adopt facet-complete exact projection over p5’s incomplete LP: audited sharp width 95 versus 100 no-IV; simulated gridwide coverage 95.1%.
